episode_thesis: Rob Carver argues that in slow, cheap-to-run systematic trend following the durable edge comes from boring, near-certain improvements (accurate costs, clean data, wide diversification, avoiding overfit) rather than from complexity, and his 12-month review (April 2025 to April 2026, +23.7%) confirms that slow trend signals did best. On allocation he explains the Quantica return-stacking result: because futures are cash efficient, diversifiers can be added on top of equities with leverage, and their size is set by correlation to equities, diversification drag and cash efficiency, not by Sharpe. On managed-futures ETFs both speakers see no clear evidence that replication beats real CTAs and warn that ten years of data and a slow-trend-friendly regime cannot settle it.

speakers.name: Rob Carver
speakers.role: independent systematic futures trader, ex-AHL, author (book due December 2026)
speakers.speaker_note: Recorded Thursday 16 April 2026. Captions are clean for the two speakers. Ledger corrections applied: his biggest exposure is long equities (small in size because overall risk is a third of target), with a reasonably sized short in bonds and a little long energy; the identical-forecast-weights practice is his, but the overfitting motive was the questioner's guess; the passage on Dunn's staff spending most time on risk management rather than signals is the host's, not his.

worldview_premises.premise: Costs are predictable year to year while performance is noise, so cost reduction is a near-certain gain (50bp of slippage saved is 50bp every year) whereas 50bp of added expected return is random; costs deserve more weight in design than performance.
worldview_premises.support: His realised costs and slippage were within one or two basis points of the prior year, validating his cost model.

worldview_premises.premise: Marginal gains add up: wide diversification, not trading too fast, accurate costs and avoiding overfit are small robust improvements that separate good CTAs from the rest; due diligence should probe operations and cost estimation, not the 'source of alpha'.
worldview_premises.support: Brailsford cycling analogy; his own practice.

worldview_premises.premise: Experienced quants prefer simple methods and know when they suffice; inexperienced highly qualified people overuse complexity (over naive mean-variance, linear regression), which can worsen results; using complex methods one does not understand, including LLMs on financial data, is the main danger.
worldview_premises.support: Nearly two decades in the CTA industry; anecdotal; the '0.01%' figure for AI users who avoid going wrong is a rhetorical estimate.

worldview_premises.premise: Slow trading means little alpha decay, so one model can run for years or decades without a big research team constantly finding new signals; performance gains come from tedious work like measuring costs and cleaning data to diversify into more markets, and PhD skills matter mainly when diversifying into options, equities or HFT.
worldview_premises.support: Experience as manager; PhD headcount partly a marketing signal.

worldview_premises.premise: Diversity of thought in a research team (economists with physicists and mathematicians) helps; origins shape style (AHL descendants designed by physicists, many US CTAs grew out of floor trading), neither better nor worse.
worldview_premises.support: He was AHL's first economist hire.

worldview_premises.premise: Diversification is not free: assets less correlated with equities tend to have lower returns, so with a fixed budget diversifying costs performance; leverage on cash-efficient diversifiers converts the higher Sharpe into higher return.
worldview_premises.support: Quantica paper (theoretical results, past performance caveat).

worldview_premises.premise: Futures are cash efficient (about 25% cash for 15% vol; his own 30-35% at 25% vol), so a CTA's cash efficiency comes from using futures, not from trend following being magic, and fully funded short-duration bonds use a lot of cash for little risk.
worldview_premises.support: His own margin usage; margin about 10% on a short US bond (from memory).

worldview_premises.premise: Allocation is buying risk with cash, so leverage can enlarge the pie instead of slicing a fixed pie.

For forward-looking allocation, assume equal Sharpe ratios across assets rather than extrapolating the equity run; fundamentally equities earn earnings yield plus inflation, and gold should return inflation plus zero because supply responds to price, swinging widely around an inflation-adjusted trend.
worldview_premises.support: Supply response in gold; 50-year inflation-adjusted chart recalled; admits not a gold expert.

worldview_premises.premise: Physical oil can decouple from benchmark futures in a supply shock because futures are tied to a grade and delivery location, so futures understate the squeeze.
worldview_premises.support: FT Alphaville article; physical oil in Sri Lanka at 286 dollars a barrel versus futures near 90-100.

worldview_premises.premise: Performance fees align managers with investors better than flat fees paid for raising assets.
worldview_premises.support: Theoretical alignment argument; no evidence given.

worldview_premises.premise: Smoother trends are easier to trade than violent moves; in the last year the slowest trend signals did best in every case, even before costs, and the core EWMAC divergent signal was the best divergent rule.
worldview_premises.support: His 12-month review, one year of data.

worldview_premises.premise: Convergent signals diversify a trend book: a multi-signal book lags pure trend in a good trend year but protected in the terrible prior year; skew-based buying of recent fat negative tails acted like a bounce strategy and added value, while carry was flat and relative carry slightly positive.
worldview_premises.support: His own results over the last 12 months.

mechanism_chains.topic: Return stacking: how much of a diversifier to add to equities

steps.from: Allocation as buying risk with cash
steps.to: Futures give risk for little cash (about 25% cash for 15% vol), so a CTA can sit on top of equities
steps.why: Futures are very cash efficient; short-duration bonds bought unlevered are not.

steps.from: Less-correlated assets have lower raw returns (diversification drag)
steps.to: With a fixed pie, diversification costs performance
steps.why: Equities were an outstanding asset class, so moving away costs return.

steps.to: Sharpe improvement is converted into higher return
steps.why: More leverage restores return while keeping the diversification benefit, as long as it is not excessive.

steps.from: Correlation to equities, diversification drag and cash efficiency
steps.to: The optimal size of the added strategy: short vol about 10% of equity, long vol over 100%, trend, gold and Treasuries about 50%
steps.why: Quantica result presented as theoretical with caveats.

mechanism_chains.evidence: Quantica paper 'If you can't beat it, stack it' (graphs, figure five); he calls results theoretical and past performance no guide.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Study periods flatter the diversifier (gold since 2000; gold futures lost 53% in the 1990s per the host); leverage too high; results depend on forward-looking return assumptions.

mechanism_chains.fails_when: Moving into options, equities or HFT needs PhD-level skills; fast trading brings alpha decay.

decision_process.practice: Vol-targeted system whose risk scales with average forecast strength: cut to about a third of long-term target when forecasts are weak; position sizing mechanically takes profit out of a bubble as volatility rises.
decision_process.why: Weak or conflicting signals mean a hard environment; risk should follow signal strength. Doubles as own trend-strength barometer.

decision_process.practice: Core EWMAC trend crossovers plus convergent signals (carry, relative carry, skew bounce); identical forecast weights for every instrument today.
decision_process.why: Treats instruments as the same for fitting (ignoring costs).

decision_process.practice: Plan: statistically test whether instrument weights differ, then pool fitting across similar instruments such as US 5 and 10 year; allow different weights only if statistical evidence supports it.
decision_process.why: At AHL each asset class team fitted its own weights, and whether that added value was an open question.

decision_process.practice: Annual review aligned to the UK tax year: benchmark raw and vol-adjusted returns against SG CTA and a same-currency fund (AHL), then break down by asset class, market and rule.
decision_process.why: Risk targets differ, and same-currency benchmark removes currency noise; margin interest (about 300bp) must be included for fairness.

decision_process.practice: Keep a modest long equities, reasonably sized short bonds and a little long energy position; net may be flat if the oil shock hits equities.
decision_process.why: Low overall risk because signals are weak; inflation-leaning mix.

decision_process.practice: Judge ETFs against a random set of actual CTAs for correlation; treat replication ETFs as acceptable but not proven.
decision_process.why: Correlation to SG CTA is built in for replication funds.

decision_process.practice: Treat guarantees of returns or outperformance as a red flag.
decision_process.why: The same language scammers impersonating CTAs use.

speakers.evidence_style: Own track record and annual review (one year, small sample), explicit benchmarks and cost data; first-principles reasoning and analogy (pizza, marginal gains); frank about what he does not know (gold, equities, ETF crisis-alpha method) and about theoretical results needing caveats.

current_views.view: The war's oil supply shock has had a muted equity reaction but will eventually matter; 100 dollar oil understates pent-up demand and lack of supply, so more upside is possible.
current_views.reasoning: Physical oil far above futures (286 dollars in Sri Lanka); his own expectation that the equity position would be hit if the shock plays out.

current_views.view: His own book: risk about a third of target, modest long equities, small long energy, reasonable short bonds; difficult market to trade; up about 5.8% year to date after a 9.5% peak in late February.
current_views.reasoning: Weak and conflicting signals after a March pullback.

current_views.view: Over the 12 months to 5 April 2026 his futures account made 23.7% (about 26% on a month-end basis), mostly in a late May to mid-October run and a metals bubble burst from late December to early January; equities and metals contributed most and bonds lost most.
current_views.reasoning: Review of his own results against SG CTA and AHL (about 30% vol adjusted each).

current_views.view: It was a good year to be over-allocated to slow trend following; the slowest signals did best everywhere, and fast trend CTAs lagged.
current_views.reasoning: Rule-by-rule review of his own signals.

speakers.name: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host, Top Traders Unplugged)
speakers.role: host; Dunn Capital-linked CTA industry commentator (speaks of 'we at Dunn', owner of a trend barometer)
speakers.speaker_note: Host, biased towards trend following (acknowledges it). Ledger correction applied: the passage that most staff effort at a CTA goes to things other than signal generation, including risk management, is his.

worldview_premises.premise: Large London CTAs share the AHL origin and similar methodology (moving average / time-series momentum), whereas US CTAs historically used breakouts; CTAs differ mainly in speed, methodology details, data handling, risk targets and the markets traded.
worldview_premises.support: Industry knowledge; says he could be wrong and will not say what he cannot back up.

worldview_premises.premise: Team size does not drive results: Dunn with one or two PhDs beat firms with fifty; what matters is a few people who handle large data sets and think differently, and most effort goes to things other than signals, including risk management.
Long-term core allocations do not need intraday dealing; the case for ETFs of CTA strategies is practical (tickers, model portfolios, tax-sheltered accounts), though he is biased towards UCITS funds.
worldview_premises.support: Own client work; no cost data.

worldview_premises.premise: Equities have been very hard to beat for 15-20 years, so the right frame is adding trend on top of equities without selling them (portable alpha / return stacking, not new but little adopted).
worldview_premises.support: History (1990s portable alpha, Standpoint 2020 launch) and Quantica paper.

worldview_premises.premise: Diversifiers should be chosen for low correlation and cash efficiency, not high Sharpe; the room to scale is what matters. Gold's strong stats depend on the sample (1990s gold futures lost 53%) and it deserves only a small allocation.
worldview_premises.support: Quantica paper; Dunn study of alternatives with equities finds only trend stands out (he acknowledges bias).

worldview_premises.premise: Replication funds compared to CTAs need adjustment for vol and interest income; after adjustment there is no outperformance; simplification removes the edge; and their slowness was flattered by the last 12 months; the article authors run real CTAs, a source bias.

speakers.evidence_style: Industry data, anecdote and published studies (including Dunn's own); open about his bias as a CTA manager.

current_views.view: Trend barometer at 55 (strong, not the strongest this year); longer-horizon trend followers cut equities in March without going short, so they benefited from the April equity rebound; metals and resource currencies resumed trending.
current_views.reasoning: Recovery in equities and metals; barometer measures aggregate CTA trend strength.

current_views.view: April 2026 data: Beta 50, SG CTA and SG Trend up about 8% YTD versus MSCI World +4.07%; short-term traders only +4.64% YTD, so faster CTAs again lagged longer-horizon trend.
current_views.reasoning: Index numbers as of Tuesday evening.

current_views.view: The S&P 500 hit a new all-time high after a roughly 10% correction (quick dip-buying); Treasury Secretary Bessent said the Fed should wait on cuts during the Iranian war, giving mixed signals with the White House.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: The Quantica allocation sizes (short vol about 10%, long vol over 100%, trend/gold/Treasuries about 50%) are presented as theoretical and hinge on forward-looking return assumptions not given in the discussion.
Claim that replication cost savings look overstated is asserted without numbers; the source blog article is cited but not quoted.
The ETF-vs-CTA study's crisis-alpha method is unexplained, and ten years has few crises; neither speaker can state its conclusion.

His benchmark comparison mixes bases: 23.7% is April-to-April, while the comparison with AHL (18.1%) and SG CTA (15.3%) used month-end figures and about 26% for himself; vol-adjusted both funds come out about 30%.
Slow trend superiority is based on one year of his own results; he calls it a good year to be over-allocated, but it is not evidence for general speed choice.
Statement that most uses of LLMs on financial data go wrong ('0.01%' not) is rhetorical with no evidence.
The Dunn study (only trend stands out among strategies combined with equities) is from the host's own firm, which he acknowledges as biased; no figures given.
Claim that 1990s gold futures lost 53% is cited from the Quantica paper while the same speakers use gold's inflation-plus-zero fundamental; no sample or contract detail given.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Carver watches signal strength (his own risk running at a third of target) and an oil supply shock that he expects to hit equities eventually; the host watches the trend barometer (55) and cross-asset trends (metals, resource currencies, equity rebound). For allocation both stress correlation to equities, diversification drag and cash efficiency over Sharpe, and a regime caveat: the past year favoured slow trend, which flatters slow replication funds. Horizons are months (trend follow-through) to decades (equal-Sharpe and inflation-plus returns).
reader_inferences: (reader) Carver's stance links three claims: costs are known, performance is noise, and signals are slow, so edge is operational; this explains why he treats cost accuracy and diversification breadth as the main sources of reliable improvement.

(reader) The return-stacking logic means a diversifier's value depends on how little cash it uses, so a bond fund bought unlevered is worse than the same exposure via futures even with the same Sharpe.
(reader) Both speakers read the last year's slow-trend dominance as regime-specific, so conclusions about replication funds (slow) and fast CTAs both need to be re-tested when faster trend works.

(reader) Carver's book is positioned inflation-leaning (long equities and energy, short bonds) yet he expects an oil shock could hit equities, implying he sees his net exposure as hedged by construction rather than as a directional call.
